data.title: Bíňa – one of the largest earthwork hillforts in the Carpathian Basin
data.excerpt: The remains of a massive earthwork fortification at Bíňa in southern Slovakia enclose more than 107 hectares — the largest continuous fortified area in Slovakia and one of the largest in the Carpathian Basin. Three circuits of ramparts, built without any internal reinforcement, crown a terrace rising up to 17 m above the Hron, and in 1983 the richest Great Moravian magnate grave in Slovakia was found here.
data.metaTitle: Bíňa – a giant earthwork hillfort above the Hron
data.metaDescription: Three circuits of ramparts at Bíňa enclose over 107 ha above the Hron: the largest fortified area in Slovakia and the seat of a 9th-century Slavic elite.

keyFacts.label: Total fortified area
keyFacts.value: 107.58 ha — the largest continuous fortified area in Slovakia and one of the largest in the Carpathian Basin

keyFacts.label: Ramparts
keyFacts.value: Three circuits, total length 5,100 m; height 4–9.40 m, width at the base 16–24 m

keyFacts.label: Ditch
keyFacts.value: Up to 11.5 m between the crest of the rampart and the bottom of the ditch

keyFacts.label: Volume of earth
keyFacts.value: c. 253,000 m³ — construction took roughly 6 months with 500 labourers

keyFacts.label: Grave of a magnate's wife (1983)
keyFacts.value: The richest Great Moravian magnate grave in Slovakia — 14 silver earrings, finger rings, gombíky, 2 small knives

keyFacts.label: Excavation
keyFacts.value: Š. Janšák (1930s), archaeologists of the 1960s, B. Chropovský, K. Pieta — dating disputed between the 9th and the late 10th century

timeline.description: A hut with pottery finds and unfinished querns, dated to the middle of the 9th century at the latest.

timeline.title: Grave with a Great Moravian pot
timeline.description: The grave above the hut contained a characteristic Great Moravian pot; the dating is also confirmed by the find of a vitreous bead in a neighbouring grave.

timeline.description: The most recent exact dating methods (confirmed also by K. Pieta in 2009) have shifted the building of the fortification to the period of Great Moravia.

timeline.title: The latest possible date for the burial of the hoard
timeline.description: Hoards of axe-shaped currency bars occur most often in the 9th century and only occasionally in the first half of the 10th century.

timeline.title: An alternative theory: Koppány's revolt
timeline.description: An older theory (Habovštiak, 1960s) dates the fortification to the time of Koppány's revolt against Stephen I — a view superseded today.

timeline.title: The foundation charter of Pannonhalma Abbey
timeline.description: It documents the historical fact of Koppány's defeat — King Stephen I endowed the monastery with estates after his victory.

timeline.title: The upper limit for dating the rampart
timeline.description: Features and graves built into the body of the rampart after its construction are dated to this period.

timeline.title: The Bzovík charter
timeline.description: It mentions that King Stephen I granted part of Bíňa to Hunt's son Bin, after whom the village received its name.

timeline.title: Archaeological excavation (Habovštiak)
timeline.description: The excavation discovered graves cut into the rampart and concluded that the rampart was of younger, post-Great Moravian origin.

timeline.title: The grave of a magnate's wife discovered
timeline.description: The richest Great Moravian magnate grave in Slovakia — a woman aged between 17 and 24.

timeline.title: Further archaeological excavation
timeline.description: More medieval graves cut into the body of the rampart were discovered.

timeline.title: K. Pieta's lecture
timeline.description: At the Vedecká cukrárnia (Science Café), PhDr. Karol Pieta confirmed the Great Moravian dating of the fortification on the basis of the latest methods.

children.text: At Bíňa in southern Slovakia lie the remains of a massive earthwork fortification, one of the largest in the Carpathian Basin. The uniqueness and sheer scale of this hillfort have long attracted the attention of historical geographers, historians and, not least, archaeologists.
The geographical setting of the site

blocks.caption: Bíňa on the 1st military survey of 1764 — it is clear where the outer rampart joined the middle one
blocks.alt: Bíňa on the 1st military survey of 1764 — it is clear where the outer rampart joined the middle one

children.text: The builders chose the site for the extensive fortification at Bíňa with great ingenuity. Nowhere in the Hron valley is there such a naturally advantageous place that would, by the laying out of rampart circuits, provide a space of the size we find precisely here. This advantage of the terrain lies not only in the isolated elevation of the terrace, which at the church in Bíňa rises as much as 17 m above the water level of the Hron and nowhere falls below 10 m, but also in the fact that a large part of this raised ground is naturally protected — on the eastern side, along the whole length of the fortified area, by the Hron and by the steep, in places almost vertical, bank of the river. The artificial fortification at Bíňa was built so as to make the best possible use of this safety given by nature and to increase it accordingly. The course of the entire artificial defensive system was laid out so that the individual belts of ramparts always linked up suitably with the natural landforms, which thus became part of the fortification system. It was also a great advantage for the builders that the soil at Bíňa is very cohesive and allowed fairly high earthen banks to be built without having to be strengthened, inside or outside, by any construction that would hold the body of the rampart together.
Description of the remains of the Bíňa hillfort

blocks.caption: Bíňa on the 2nd military survey from the mid-19th century. The ramparts are clearly visible
blocks.alt: Bíňa on the 2nd military survey from the mid-19th century. The ramparts are clearly visible

children.text: The total area enclosed by the ramparts is over 107 ha and the combined length of all three rampart circuits is 5,100 m. This is therefore an area matched by none of the hitherto known hillforts of an economic-administrative or military-defensive character from the so-called hillfort period in Slovakia, the Czech lands or the nearest neighbouring states. Occupation of the fortified area is concentrated only on the raised parts of the Hron terrace, between the western bank of the Hron and the former inner rampart. Only in the northern part, around the former manor house, does the occupation extend beyond the inner rampart as well, that is, to places that were often settled as early as prehistory and to which the later medieval and modern occupation was also tied. This area, which was usually used for more permanent occupation, is only a small part, roughly a fifth, of the total fortified area. The space between the outer and the inner rampart, which makes up the rest, an area about four times larger, shows no traces of more permanent occupation either from the time close to the building of the ramparts or from later centuries.
The outer rampart

The ramparts of the Bíňa hillfort were investigated and excellently described as early as the 1930s by – who else – Štefan Janšák. Along the whole southern and south-western part this rampart was partly built on the northern bank of a gully, which the builders used both to increase the security of the fortification and to save labour. The gully touched the rampart at its outer foot and, with its natural depth of 4 to 6 m, contributed considerably to the inaccessibility of the rampart. Where the rampart once stood there remains today a natural gentle slope descending to the brook. Along the northern bank of the brook, at right angles to the slope, a narrow lane runs from west to east down to the Hron. On one stretch the rampart is cut through by the road leading from Bíňa to Kamenín and Štúrovo. The fairly deep bed of the brook is spanned here by a bridge. The rampart is therefore completely missing in this part. The rampart is flattened, on the southern side partly dug away along its length and on the northern side pushed out into the neighbouring gardens and houses. Over a short stretch it has so far retained a slight elevation above the adjacent gardens. On the southern side the rampart slopes down into the natural gully and the crest of the rampart rises as much as 6.40 m above the bottom of the gully. In several parts the rampart has already been completely dug away and the material carted off. Small houses stand sparsely in its place. A large clay pit was created in one part of the rampart and was still in use in the 1970s. On the stretch between the 620th and the 700th metre there was still, in 1934, that is at the time when Janšák's description of the Bíňa ramparts was being compiled, an 80 m long stretch of surviving rampart, but that too is missing today. The original rampart on the stretch between the 800th and the 1,100th metre already ran outside today's village and was on completely level ground. On the south-western side, outwards, a ditch runs along the rampart, from which the material for building the rampart was taken. In several further places the rampart is pierced by openings created in modern times. It is, however, possible to come across stretches that have remained very well preserved, so that they allow adequate investigation.

children.text: The middle rampart

This rampart was partly built along a natural gully. Its southern slope has survived along almost its whole length. Houses and gardens stand on part of this rampart too. Further on, the rampart is interrupted by the state road. In some places the rampart has been completely removed, the bed of the gully filled in, and the buildings of the local school stand in their place. Around the school, north of the road, a smaller step 1–2 m high can be made out, which is the only trace here of the former fortification. In the following stretches the former ditch of the inner rampart can be made out in some places. At the 1,250th metre a slight bend of the remnant of the rampart towards the east can be seen, by which the middle rampart probably joined the outer rampart.
The inner rampart

At a distance of 100 m from point 0 by the middle rampart, towards the north, there is again a natural incision into the Hron terrace, opening into the Hron as a fairly deep but dry gully. On the northern bank of this gully the inner rampart of the fortification once stood, and at point 0 it linked up with the Hron. In the next stretch, where the state road cuts across the presumed rampart in a gentle bend, and around it, in the wider, so far unbuilt space which forms a kind of village green here, the ground is so levelled and modified that all traces and indications of the rampart and the ditch have completely disappeared. To the north-west of the state road, where the ground is built over or laid out as gardens, there are likewise no traces of the rampart. Only on the stretch from the 240th to the 330th metre can indications of a shallow and broad hollow be seen, which then shows more clearly further to the north on the stretch between the 620th and the 720th metre, where its bottom and steep slopes are preserved almost in their original state. We can identify it with certainty as the former ditch of the inner rampart, which lay to the east of it.

blocks.caption: A section through the rampart clearly showing where the palisade was set
blocks.alt: A section through the rampart clearly showing where the palisade was set

children.text: From the description of the ramparts and from the drawings of their situation on the ground it can be read that the builders followed a certain principle: with a triple circuit of ramparts they wanted to protect the highest part of the terrace around the church. Although the rest of the terrace is almost flat, they did not build three perfectly parallel semi-elliptical ramparts, but used the configuration of the terrain, partly in order to increase the inaccessibility of the ramparts and thus to prevent, or make as difficult as possible, entry into the fortified area, and partly in order to make the work more economical. This was achieved by leading the ramparts above the natural gullies. That is why the distance of the southern end of the outer rampart from the southern end of the middle rampart is great, whereas between the two southern ends of the middle and the inner rampart there are only 100 m. In the north the middle rampart does not join the Hron terrace — as the other two ramparts do — but only the outer rampart, because here it was possible to make use of the brook and the adjacent marshes to the north of the rampart. Both ramparts have considerable dimensions in their better-preserved parts. At the foot their width is around 22–28 m and their height around 8–9 m. In two places the ramparts form a kind of saddle, namely between the 1,420th and the 1,600th metre at the outer rampart and between the 900th and the 1,000th metre at the middle rampart. It is interesting that the ditch is also considerably shallower in these places, and at the outer rampart it is missing altogether. A secondary approach into the fortified area may have led in this direction, even though the main entrance gateways must have lain in accordance with the direction of the main route in the Hron valley, which passes here from south to north roughly along the places followed by today's state road.

blocks.alt: A section through the rampart after Š. Janšák

children.text: According to Š. Janšák's calculation, the area of the fortified space between the Hron and the outer rampart is 107.58 ha, of which the enclosure between the middle and the outer rampart accounts for roughly 65 ha and the area between the Hron terrace and the middle rampart for 42.58 ha. The area enclosed by the inner rampart and the bank of the Hron may have been around 15.60 ha. The volume of earth that had to be heaped into the body of the ramparts during their construction amounts to c. 253,000 m³. This work took roughly 6 months with 500 labourers achieving a daily output of 3 m³. In its extent it is the largest continuous fortified area in Slovakia and one of the largest in the whole Carpathian Basin.

The entire inner rampart has been dismantled and carted away for almost 100 years, so its relationship to the older settlement layer cannot be assessed. In the vicinity of the more recent cuts through the other two ramparts, no cultural remains could be detected beneath their banks.
The construction of the ramparts

The Bíňa fortification is an exceptional phenomenon among the other Slavic hillforts in the territory of Slovakia, because not one of the ramparts contains any internal reinforcement or any other construction (typical of other hillforts) that would hold the body of the rampart together. The body of the rampart here was heaped up from brownish-yellow loess mixed with more or less grey humic soil. Layers of relatively clean and sterile loess alternated irregularly with obliquely laid thinner and thicker layers of heaped humus. On the other hand, it must be said that the soil at Bíňa is of such quality and so compact that it has been able to hold the relatively steep slopes of the ramparts to this day. A wooden palisade was probably placed on top of the rampart, and its traces can be clearly seen in the sections through the rampart from more recent excavations. The absence of a feature typical of Great Moravian hillforts – of any rampart construction at all – even led archaeologists in the 1960s to the conclusion that the Bíňa hillfort was built only after the fall of Great Moravia and that it is not a typical Slavic hillfort but a fortress built by King Stephen at the time of his war against Koppány. At the same time, however, he admits elsewhere that the rampart could have arisen after the middle of the 9th century, which would still fit within the flowering of Great Moravia. The most recent research at the hillfort has likewise shifted the dating of the Bíňa fortification to the Great Moravian period (the 9th century). One of the most important Slovak archaeologists, PhDr. Karol Pieta, DrSc., stated unambiguously in the
Vedecká cukrárnia (Science Café)

on 27 October 2009, for example, that the most recent exact dating methods have shifted the building of the Bíňa fortification to the time of the existence of Great Moravia (see around minutes 46–48). The insights and conclusions about the possibilities of dating the Bíňa defensive system were obtained only at the northern part of the outer rampart and at one part of the middle rampart. The inner rampart could not be dated more precisely, but it can presumably be logically assumed that this rampart is not younger than the other two ramparts.

In all the surviving stretches the ramparts are characterised by the striking massiveness of the bank, which reaches a height of 4–9.40 m and a width of 16–24 m at the base. The dimensions of the rampart vary only according to where and on what kind of place it is built, i.e. the height of the artificial bank tends to be lower if it was heaped up at the edge of a natural step on the ground, and greater if it was built on level ground. Other differences in the shape and appearance of the ramparts are merely the result of later interventions. The remains of the whole Bíňa fortification are likewise characterised by a massive ditch on the outer side of the ramparts. Its size too was adapted to the configuration of the terrain. From the surviving remains of the ditch at the former inner rampart, which has now been completely dismantled, it can be judged that this rampart too had approximately the same profile and appearance as the surviving parts of the middle and outer ramparts.

As for the ditch in front of the rampart, it was established that the original bottom of the ditch was a further 280 cm deeper than the present level of its bottom, which even today is of considerable depth in relation to the surrounding terrain — 4 m. Such a difference in height between the present crest of the rampart and the identified base of the ditch amounts to 11.5 m. In the period shortly after the ramparts were built this difference must have been considerably greater, because the original height of the rampart was also greater, by at least 2 m. The slopes of the ditch converged towards the bottom and passed into a slightly rounded, relatively narrow bottom.
Archaeological excavation of the Bíňa fortification

In some parts of the rampart, graves cut into the body of the rampart during the Middle Ages were discovered both during the excavation in the 1960s and in 2008. Further, the remains of several huts — semi-sunken buildings — dated to the Great Moravian period were discovered within the hillfort. In one of them, remains of the original walls of smoothed and hardened loess survived in places. Along the individual walls, distinct traces of posts also survived in the form of smaller circular pits; in one of them — in the south-western corner of the hut — the remains of charred wood from the post also survived. In the upper part of the fill of the hut, 27 fragments of stone were found. On several of them, traces of working into the shape of querns can be seen, which were, however, not finished, because during the work the stone either broke or the product was spoiled in some other way and its working was not continued. Accordingly, it seems that a quern maker worked in the vicinity of the hut and threw the failed and spoiled, or broken, querns into the hut, which was already abandoned by then. The find is striking evidence of specialised quern production at this site in the Great Moravian period. Many pottery sherds were discovered in the hut. The remains of a simple pottery kiln were also discovered. The vessels from which the sherds found here come were fired in it as well.

Directly beneath the crest of the rampart bank a bowl-shaped depression was found — a feature 155 cm in diameter and reaching a depth of 26 cm. This was most likely some kind of production feature where work was done with strong heat. The strongly burnt walls of the feature testify to this. Not far from this feature a grain pit was identified, in which diagnostic fragments of pots decorated with a wavy line were found. Another feature is part of a hut, a semi-sunken building, in which the remains of a hearth were identified. The features described were covered by the rampart bank. On the basis of these observations, archaeologists in the 1960s concluded that the rampart was relatively younger than the remains found beneath it. The upper limit for dating the rampart, in turn, is formed by the features and graves which were evidently built into the body of the rampart after its construction and which are dated to the beginning of the second half of the 12th century.
The most interesting finds from the Bíňa hillfort

Within the hillfort, remains from the Great Moravian period, the Migration Period, the Roman provincial period, the La Tène period and the Neolithic have thus been documented. The Great Moravian period indicated above is revealed at first glance by the character of the settlement features — huts and features connected with the occupation (a grain pit and the like). The settlement features were square dwellings sunk into the ground with a hearth or a fireplace in one of the corners. Such dwellings are typical and characteristic of the Great Moravian period across the wide territory inhabited by the Slavs, especially in lowland environments. One of the features — a hut — had a recess at its south-eastern corner, projecting southwards from its probably square outline. Judging by the strongly burnt inner walls, this can only have been an oven, which was fairly large and could therefore have served not only for heating the living space but also for baking bread. In not a single case were objects found in the features that their inhabitants would have left there because they had perhaps to abandon the dwelling suddenly as a result of some catastrophe. All the dwellings, it seems, were abandoned deliberately, and nothing of the original furnishings was therefore found in them.

A large number of sherds were found at the site, mostly from pot-shaped and occasionally also bottle-shaped vessels with a simple rounded or vertically cut rim, sometimes forming a fine groove on the inner side. Sherds from the walls and bases of the vessels reveal manufacture by the wheel-finishing technique, that is, on a hand-turned potter's wheel. Their decoration most often consisted of a single or multiple incised wavy line combined with dense bands of circumferential grooves, or of a shallowly incised circumferential spiral line.
The hoard of currency bars

In the north-western corner of one of the Great Moravian huts, above a grave that had been dug beneath its floor, a hoard of iron currency bars was found. This hoard is a considerably more reliable means of dating than the pottery. Hoards of axe-shaped currency bars occur in our area most often in the 9th century and only occasionally still in the first half of the 10th century. The middle of the 10th century can therefore be regarded as the latest possible date at which the Bíňa hoard could have been placed in the ground. Some time before the hoard was buried, a grave was dug in the same place, which disturbed the floor and part of the fireplace in the hut. Since the grave was identified very shallowly below the level of the floor, it must be assumed that it was dug here at a time when the sunken space of the hut had already been at least partly filled in. The hut and the fragments of pottery that found their way into it secondarily must therefore be at least 5–10 years older than the grave. And the grave itself, quite apart from the fact that the hoard of currency bars lay above it, can be dated at the latest to the second half of the 9th century, because a characteristic Great Moravian pot was found in it. Such a dating is also confirmed by the find of a vitreous bead in one of the neighbouring graves, which belong to the same chronological horizon as the grave in the hut; such beads have so far occurred only in cemeteries of the Great Moravian and earlier periods. From the above it clearly follows that the hut, together with the pottery finds and the fragments of unfinished querns in its fill, can be dated at the latest to the middle of the 9th century.
The grave of the wife of a Slavic magnate

Of all the Great Moravian magnate graves that have been found in the territory of the Slovak Republic, the richest is precisely the one at Bíňa. It was discovered in 1983. It is a grave in which a woman aged between 17 and 24 was buried. It contained 14 silver earrings, a silver and a bronze finger ring, and also four silver repoussé gombíky. This exceptionally rich assemblage was completed by two small iron knives. The jewellery found in this grave was worn by members of the wealthiest magnate families known to us from the Great Moravian centres at Mikulčice or at Staré Město near Uherské Hradiště. It is possible that the buried woman was a member of a noble family from Nitra or from Moravia who married into Bíňa. The fact that there was a sufficiently dignified setting here for the life of such a wealthy lady points to the position of Bíňa in the 9th century as the seat of a Slavic elite controlling the lower Hron region.

In the Great Moravian period, then, there was a very large and important occupation at Bíňa (in one of the ten huts uncovered so far, striking evidence of local quern production was also found). From the period after the fall of Great Moravia we find here neither archaeological nor historical evidence of a need that would have called for such a massive and extensive fortification. Traces of occupation from this period are indeed present here, roughly in the same places to which the earlier occupation was also tied, but they do not so far point to any special position of Bíňa in this period.

As already mentioned above, archaeologists in the 1960s came to the conclusion that the Bíňa fortification did not have the character of an ordinary hillfort with some important economic-administrative and central position for a particular territorial unit, like the known Great Moravian and later hillforts in the territory of Slovakia, Moravia, Bohemia, Poland, the USSR and Germany. They judged that this was rather a fortification whose construction was called for by some sudden and temporary need, which did not follow on from the earlier significance of the site and which did not substantially influence the further development of its occupation either.

One of the views is that the Bíňa fortification arose at the time of the advance of the Hungarian nomadic and warrior tribes into the interior of the present-day territory of Slovakia, which falls roughly in the first decades of the 10th century. Š. Janšák already attempted this, relying mainly on the account of Anonymus, according to which the Magyars halted at a certain earthen stronghold called Varod as they penetrated into the territory of Slovakia up the Hron region. B. Chropovský too, in his study of Slavic hillforts in Slovakia, inclines to the older views that the Bíňa hillfort was built before the arrival of the Magyars, relying on the fact that there was already an important settlement centre at Bíňa in the Great Moravian period. As has already been mentioned above, however, modern archaeology has come to the conclusion that the massive fortification of the Bíňa hillfort is of Great Moravian origin.
Did Stephen I build the fortification together with Hunt and Poznan?

The representative of an older, now superseded view is the theory that the Bíňa fortification arose only at the time of Koppány's revolt against Stephen at the end of the 10th century, a view set out in detail by Habovštiak in the 1960s. For interest's sake I present this view as well. I must point out, however, that Habovštiak himself drew attention to the fact that such an explanation is not definitive and that further research will be needed to verify its credibility.

A connection between the Bíňa fortification and this event is also indirectly suggested by an older tradition recorded as early as Matej Bel, who, however, seemed to want to weaken the credibility of this tradition himself and expressed a certain doubt about its truthfulness. This doubt is indeed justified, because according to the course of events during Koppány's revolt it is not likely that Koppány could have been staying in Slovakia at that time; his domain was the territory on the northern shore of Lake Balaton around Veszprém, and he himself resided at Somogyvár. If, then, we are still to regard the tradition mentioned as a kind of source for explaining the function of the Bíňa hillfort, we can understand it at most as revealing and indicating only the time when the fortification arose; as regards its originator, however, Stephen I, or rather his supporters, is more likely to be reckoned with here, and not Koppány.

This assumption finds support in the medieval Hungarian chronicles of the 13th–15th centuries, which, when they describe the war of Stephen I against the Somogy duke Koppány, state literally: “When Stephen had assembled an army, he set out against his enemy and was girded with the sword by the river Hron. There he appointed as his bodyguards two magnates (of Slovak origin, note by Orgoň), Hunt and Poznan.” Likewise the medieval Hungarian chroniclers, describing the Hunt and Poznan families, say: “Hunt and Poznan also came, who girded St Stephen with the sword in the river Hron according to German custom”. From the above it can clearly be seen that King Stephen I was staying at the time of Koppány's revolt somewhere above the Danube on the bank of the Hron, though certainly not far from Esztergom, which was his birthplace and his seat. It is true, however, that it is questionable how far the information of the medieval chronicles can be believed here and how far Stephen's camp can be located precisely at Bíňa. Koppány's revolt and its successful suppression by the armies and supporters of King Stephen I in 997–998 is a historical fact, documented above all in the foundation charter of Pannonhalma Abbey of 1001. By it King Stephen I endowed the monastery of Pannonhalma with extensive estates, mostly in the territory previously occupied by his opponent Koppány, in order to fulfil the vow he had made before Koppány's defeat. The chronicler's mention, however, that King Stephen I was girded with the sword by the river Hron before his armed encounter with Koppány as a sign of recognition of his coming of age is no longer so unambiguous that we could, without further investigation, interpret it as meaning that this happened precisely at Bíňa.

There are, however, further arguments to support such a possibility, especially if we assess the overall situation from a broader perspective. In the initial stage of the revolt, King Stephen I could not be entirely certain of his moral and numerical superiority and of future victory over Koppány, as is ultimately testified by his vow that if he defeated him he would build a monastery at Pannonhalma and endow it richly with estates, which he later also fulfilled. Koppány had, after all, many supporters on his side. He gathered around himself those members of the Old Hungarian tribal confederation who did not approve of King Stephen I's efforts and plans to put an end to the nomadic way of life, to turn to Christianity and to Western civilisation in general, nor of his endeavour to build a firm feudal state. These were, then, adherents of the old pastoral-nomadic free life, with whom even the later Hungarian kings had difficulties for a long time. It is therefore possible and understandable that in these times, rather uncertain for him, Stephen I made use of the support of the local Slavic magnate families — the Hunt and Poznan kindreds — and of some foreign warriors (Vencellin), and had a large fortified earthen camp built, which served to gather a larger number of troops together with their armament and equipment in one place (given the intelligence and organisational possibilities of the time this is entirely understandable) and which at the same time would be a suitable and safe refuge should the enemy's superiority temporarily prevail.

The reason for gathering the army precisely above the Danube was perhaps also Stephen I's wish that his supporters should be separated by this river from the southern areas of the country, where Koppány's influence and sympathy for him spread relatively quickly. The placing of such a camp precisely at Bíňa may have been advantageous from several points of view. It was a place that ruled out the possibility of a sudden attack from the south (a good natural obstacle was formed here by the Danube) and at the same time it was close to Esztergom, so that in good visibility contact could be maintained with it by means of signals. Finally, by its natural position too this place was advantageous and suitable for building a fortified military camp (three natural gullies on the southern side of the village, a position dominating the surrounding terrain). The division of the fortified area into three parts by three semicircular circuits of rampart banks can be explained partly by the requirement of a more perfect defence and partly by the need for the separate encampment of commanders, rank-and-file warriors, horses and cattle with provisions and battle equipment. Habovštiak further states that the building of the fortification was also within the technical capabilities of Stephen's army, and that with about 1,000 labourers and an output of approximately 3 m³ of earth per man per working day it could have been completed in roughly three months, which after all is not such a long time that we could not assume the fortification here to have arisen — particularly at a time of threat.

On this occasion, however, it is necessary to reflect on the problem of the building of earthen fortifications among the Magyars in general. We know of the Old Hungarians from Leo the Wise that the building of earthen and other more permanent fortifications was not their custom. Nor was it required by their manner of fighting, which Leo the Wise characterises as fighting by sudden attack, without any regular arrangement or ordering. This fact is also strikingly apparent in archaeology, which so far knows of no stronghold or hillfort built by members of the Hungarian tribal confederation during their occupation of the Danube region and their military campaigns to the west. The building of fortifications was therefore evidently carried out with the help of the local population, from whom the Magyars could also have adopted some of the techniques for building such works.

As regards the period to which the building of the Bíňa fortification by Stephen I was also assigned, i.e. the end of the 10th century, we so far have no evidence in Slovakia of similar structures. This fact is in turn one of the arguments against dating the Bíňa fortification to the period after the fall of Great Moravia. A further argument may also be the question of whether Stephen really needed to protect his certainly very numerous army with such an extensive and demanding fortification.

One more fact is worth mentioning, which may be connected with what the narrative sources referred to above suggest. It is the fact that King Stephen I granted part of Bíňa to Hunt's son Bin, after whom the village also received its name. We learn of this from the Bzovík charter of 1135. This endowment of Hunt's son with part of Bíňa may also in a certain sense be connected with Stephen I's desire to repay the Hunt family for the help provided, precisely with this territory, which was settled and with which his gratitude towards the Hunt family was associated more than with others.
